extracted.intended_audience: general readers of translated Indian folktales / readers interested in traditional social norms embedded in narrative
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and records prescriptive social, legal, and domestic criteria embedded in a Vikram-Betaal folktale passage (marriage eligibility rules, punishments in Dharma-Shastra, parenting cautions, and related norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dharma-Shastra punishment for perfidious dependent persons
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If a Brahman, a cow, a woman, a child, or any other person whatsoever who may be dependent on us, should be guilty of a perfidious act, their punishment is that they be banished the country.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However much they may deserve death, we must not spill their blood, as Lakshmi flies in horror from the deed. (Narrative guidance explaining that banishment, not capital punishment, is the prescribed penalty for such dependents according to the Dharma-Shastra.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Genealogical eligibility for marriage (shastra rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘She who is not descended from his paternal or maternal ancestors within the sixth degree is eligible by a high caste man for nuptials.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear rule of consanguinity: a prospective bride must not be related within six degrees on either paternal or maternal lines for a high-caste man to marry her (presented as authoritative scriptural guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Family disqualifications to avoid in choosing a wife
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In taking a wife let him studiously avoid the following families, be they ever so great, or ever so rich in kine, goats, sheep, gold, or grain: the family which has omitted prescribed acts of devotion; that which has produced no male children; that in which the Veda (scripture) has not been read; that which has thick hair on the body; and that in which members have been subject to hereditary disease.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists specific family-level red flags: lapse in religious observance, lack of male offspring, ignorance of Vedic scripture, bodily traits (excessive body hair), and hereditary disease. These are offered as categorical disqualifiers regardless of material wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/physical qualities to prefer in a wife
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance enumerating desirable attributes: ‘a girl whose person has no defect; who has an agreeable name; who walks gracefully, like a young elephant; whose hair and teeth are moderate in quantity and in size; and whose body is of exquisite softness,’ with further poetical comparisons (nose like sesame flower, eyes like lotus leaf, lips like young mango leaves, voice like the cuckoo, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A detailed set of preferred physical and comportmental traits—appearance, gait, voice, moderation of features—given as criteria for selecting an ideal spouse. The text supplies illustrative similes and an extended descriptive ideal (colour, nose, legs, eyebrows, lips, gait, hair, teeth, throat, flanks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding parenting errors: over-vigilance and under-vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘O king! men commit two capital mistakes in rearing the “domestic calamity,” and these are over-vigilance and under-vigilance.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Over-vigilance (constant suspicion) provokes rebellious wickedness in daughters; under-vigilance (neglect, idleness, freedom to associate with the wicked) breeds opportunity for vice. The passage frames these as the two main parenting errors leading to moral corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of parents (classification) and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents may be divided into three kinds: (1) the parent of many ideas—amusing, pleasant, poor, idol of children; (2) the parent with one idea and a half—temporarily indulgent but not lasting; (3) the one-idea parent—unyielding, set in opinion, resistant to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive typology used to evaluate parental character and likely effects on children: the first is indulgent/popular, the second experiments with kindness briefly, the third is inflexible and unteachable. The narrator notes strengths and weaknesses (e.g., usefulness in labor, intractability in old age) as guidance for judging parental styles.
